title: Rejection sampling — rand7 → rand10, explained first

aiGuide.intro: Short code, and the reported instruction is "explain the maths first". Use the AI to **check** your reasoning, never to produce it.
plan: Explain uniformity out loud: 49 pairs, keep 40, reject 9
AI checks your maths — no code
AI implements exactly your method; you enumerate all 49 pairs
Generalise: UniformBelow(n, m) — you state k and the limit
Follow-ups: expected calls, recycling leftover randomness

stages.name: rand7 → rand10
stages.yours: Explain before any code: two calls give **49 equally likely pairs**; number them 1–49; keep **1–40** (4 per output) and map `(cell-1) % 10 + 1`; reject 41–49 and retry. Expected rand7 calls: 2 × 49/40 ≈ **2.45**.
stages.ai: **AI checks you** first (no code), then **co-generates** exactly your method.
bad: `(rand7() + rand7()) % 10 + 1`. Sums are not uniform: over all 49 pairs, 9 comes up 7 times and 2 only 4.
It produced the maths for you — wrongly
good:
Check my reasoning, no code: two rand7 calls give 49 equally likely (row, col) pairs; I accept cells 1–40 and return (cell-1) % 10 + 1, rejecting 41–49 and retrying. Is every output exactly 4/49 per attempt? What is the expected number of rand7 calls?
— then —
Now implement exactly that as Sampling.Rand10(Func<int> rand7). Keep my signature exactly.
stages.reply: Typical defect (verified planted flaw R6): **sum-then-mod**. Or `rand7() * rand7()` — products are even less uniform.
validate: Enumerate all 49 first-try pairs: each output exactly 4 times
Rejected pairs (41–49) retry; results always in 1..10
Expected calls ≈ 2.45; worst case unbounded — say it
Sampled check: each value within a few % of 10%
stages.fix: Sum-then-mod is a different algorithm → **reject and re-prompt** with your method.
stages.say: "Every output comes from exactly four of the forty accepted cells, so it is uniform; about 2.45 calls on average, unbounded in the worst case."
stages.require: Implement `Sampling.Rand10(rand7)`. The test enumerates every outcome exactly, so "close to uniform" fails.
stages.say_iv: You have rand7(), uniform on 1 to 7. Give me rand10(), uniform on 1 to 10. Explain it mathematically before you write code.

stages.name: Generalise it
stages.yours: State it before prompting: with a source of 0..m−1, take **k** draws where m^k ≥ n, read them as a base-m number v, accept v below **the largest multiple of n** that fits, return v mod n.
bad: Make it work for any n.
`source() % n` — biased whenever m is not a multiple of n.
Modulo bias is exactly the bug this question is about
good: Implement Sampling.UniformBelow(int n, int m, Func<int> source), where source returns 0..m-1 uniformly. Find the smallest k with m^k >= n. Each attempt: k draws, combined most-significant first into v in [0, m^k). limit = m^k - (m^k % n). If v < limit return v % n, else retry. Exactly k draws per attempt. Keep my Rand10 unchanged; no plain source() % n. Explain the expected number of attempts. Show only UniformBelow.
stages.reply: Typical defect: limit computed as **n** instead of the largest multiple of n — correct but rejects far more often than needed.
validate: n = 6, m = 2: 3 draws, 6 of 8 three-bit strings accepted
Each of 0..5 produced by exactly one accepted string
Expected attempts = m^k / limit — say it
stages.fix: Limit = n → **by hand**: `limit = range - range % n`.
stages.say: "Keep the largest multiple of n that fits, so every output has the same number of accepted strings."
stages.require: Add `Sampling.UniformBelow(int n, int m, Func<int> source)`: source returns uniform values in [0, m); return uniform in [0, n).
stages.say_iv: Generalise: uniform on [0, n) from any uniform source on [0, m). For example rand01 → rand06.
